az_aegir.blurb: Aegir is a steep formation near the Reef of Rocks on the upper part of the Catalina Highway, high on Mount Lemmon above Tucson. It carries a mix of bolted face climbs and trad lines, from finger cracks and flakes to long adventurous pitches, and the grades run hard: most of the climbs are 5.11 and 5.12, with a few 5.13 and 5.14- projects for the strong. Crankbugs, Reef Break and Batten Down the Hatch are among the standouts. The elevation keeps it cooler than the desert floor. The base is reached by a ledge system, so expect some exposed scrambling before you rack up.
az_aegir.approach: Descend the gully used for the Reef of Rocks, then follow the wide ledge that cuts across the formations. A short third-class step around a corner brings Aegir into view; keep along the ledge to the foot of the routes.

az_tufa_city.blurb: Tufa City is one of the best-known walls in The Homestead, a remote limestone canyon in the desert of central Arizona. The name comes from the tufa formations that streak the face, which give pulling on pockets and columns a character rare in this part of the country. It is all bolted sport climbing with a hard bias: most routes fall in the 5.12 range, with plenty of 5.11 and a handful of 5.13s. Tufa Yard Dash and Micro Burst are favorites. It is a winter and shoulder-season destination; summer heat and monsoon storms make the canyon unpleasant.
az_tufa_city.parking_note: Turn off Highway 77 south of Globe onto the rough dirt road; a high-clearance vehicle makes the drive easier. Leave the car at the Access Fund trailhead by the upper camping area and continue on foot.
az_tufa_city.approach: From the trailhead kiosk, take the brief path out to the dirt road, follow it until a sign marks the crag trail, then keep left and uphill where it splits.

az_entrance_boulders_3.blurb: The Entrance Boulders are part of the Oak Flat bouldering zone in Queen Creek Canyon, east of Phoenix near Superior. The stone is welded volcanic tuff, grippy but abrasive, with pockets, sharp crimps and small edges that reward careful footwork and tape. This group leans toward the friendly end: about half the problems are V0 and most of the rest sit between V1 and V3, with a few harder ones. Rebirth, at V6, is the standout. Some of the taller problems in the zone carry old top-rope bolts, so judge landings carefully, and expect the holds to sometimes feel hollow or crumbly.

az_upper_wall_3.blurb: The Upper Wall is a tall quartzite face in Spring Creek, a side branch of the Christopher Creek Gorge east of Payson. It holds a mix of traditional lines and bolted routes, mostly in the 5.7 to 5.11 range, with the bulk at 5.9 and 5.10. Rodin, The Big Lebowski and Hummer Day are good places to start. The wall is at its best for morning climbing in spring and fall, and works as a comfortable winter spot later in the day. The approach crosses the creek or wash, so water level can matter.
az_upper_wall_3.parking_note: Drive east from Payson on Highway 260 to about milepost 270.8 and take the paved pull-off on the right. Leave the car on the pavement edge without blocking the road.
az_upper_wall_3.approach: Head southeast across the open field to a slim path that leaves its far edge and winds through boulders. Follow the cairned slab down into Spring Creek, cross the water, then follow the quartzite shelf along the creek to the wall.

az_boot_hill.blurb: Boot Hill is a north-facing cliff on the lower Catalina Highway on Mount Lemmon, above the Prison Camp area near Tucson. Most routes sit on the north and west faces, so the wall stays shaded for much of the day. That makes it a good choice at low elevation when the desert is warm: early spring, late fall and mild winter days. The climbing is a mix of bolted and trad lines, with a lot of moderate 5.7 to 5.10 routes and a few easier ones. Rock quality ranges from solid to crumbly, so test holds and watch for loose blocks.
az_boot_hill.parking_note: Use the southernmost parking area at the Prison Camp Campground off the lower Catalina Highway.
az_boot_hill.approach: Walk up the fire break as far as it goes, then follow the cairned trail steeply uphill to the cliff. The main branch leads to the Brickyard area near the middle of the routes.

az_south_wall_3.blurb: The South Wall is the main event at The Grail, a limestone canyon on the Arizona Strip near the Nevada line. The wall is tall, orange and blue, and vertical to slightly overhanging, with square-cut holds on sustained endurance lines. Most routes are 5.12, with a good cluster of 5.13 on the left and a few moderates near the entrance. Many longer climbs are done as single pitches with a midway anchor. Mantis, The Honeycomb and Homeostasis are good tick targets. The wall is mostly shaded, with a little morning sun in spring and summer. Bring plenty of quickdraws.
az_south_wall_3.parking_note: The canyon sits at the end of a long dirt road, and the last few miles are rough, so a high-clearance 4WD vehicle is advised. Park in the lot at the foot of the canyon.
az_south_wall_3.approach: Follow the trail up from the lot and take the right branch toward The Grail. The South Wall is the first wall in the bowl, on your right.

az_north_end.blurb: The North End is the northern section of Peaks Crag, a dacite cliff in the aspen and ponderosa forest on the San Francisco Peaks above Flagstaff. The rock is volcanic and weathered, and the cliff is streaked with color; fall is especially pretty. Most of the climbing here is bolted, with a handful of trad lines, and the grades cluster at 5.11 and 5.12 with a few 5.13s and easier warm-ups. Chasing Dragons, Black Swan and 16 Weeks are well-known routes. It is a sustained, mostly advanced crag reached by a forest hike.
az_north_end.approach: Follow the climbers' trail through the pines and aspens straight to the main wall; the North End is the left-hand (northern) portion of it.

az_parking_area_bouldering.blurb: These are the boulders closest to the parking lot at Priest Draw, a limestone bouldering area a few miles south of Flagstaff at about 7,000 feet. The stone is pocketed, and the area is famous for steep roofs, so the style can feel unusual at first. Problems range widely from V0 to the V12 level, with the largest group around V4. The Yoker, Tin Ho! and Street Fighter are among the best known. Several walls and a puzzle-shaped boulder are a minute from the car; the big roofs take 15 to 20 minutes of walking. Overhanging problems stay drier than vertical walls, which can be slick or snowy for months.
az_parking_area_bouldering.parking_note: A dirt road leads in several miles from the Lake Mary Road side to a dedicated lot at the end; the final stretch is rough, so some ground clearance helps.

az_oaklands.blurb: Oaklands is a 60 to 80 foot dacite cliff on the west side of Mount Elden above Flagstaff, named for the oaks on the gully's slope. Expect upright, precise climbing with hard individual moves on small, heavily textured holds, with a mix of bolted lines, cracks and a few mixed routes. Most routes are 5.11 and 5.12, with a few 5.13s. Runaway Train, Up the 9 and Red Dream are popular. The wall faces south, so it is warm: fall is the best time, and sunny winter days can also work.
az_oaklands.approach: From the pullout, hike east toward the mountain along the trails to the mouth of the gully, then follow the cairned climbers' trail up to the cliff.
